results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included; probable disease requires four groups (or three with a teratoma) of rapid onset plus an abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: All patients had antibodies in CSF, whereas about 14% were negative in serum; CSF titres related more closely to outcome than serum titres.
results.source: Gresa-Arribas N et al. Lancet Neurol 2014;13:167-177

results.finding: 38% had a tumour, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumour removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

results.finding: Extreme delta brush was found in 7 of 23 adults with anti-NMDAR encephalitis and was associated with a more prolonged illness.

output.summary: Published criteria and cohort data on anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: definite diagnosis rests on CSF IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies; first-line immunotherapy and tumour removal are followed by second-line agents when there is no response.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Serum anti-GluN1 positive (1:128); sodium 133 mmol/L (mild hyponatraemia); thyroid function, thyroid antibodies and other neuronal antibodies negative; beta-hCG negative
action_criteria.label: Obtain the reviewed serum work-up, including a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay that must be interpreted with CSF rather than alone
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes metabolic, endocrine, toxic and infective mimics and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, which is read with the CSF assay.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Bilateral medial temporal (right greater than left) and right insular-opercular FLAIR hyperintensity without restricted diffusion, haemorrhage or enhancement; no structural lesion
action_criteria.label: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI to exclude HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination; a normal MRI does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis
action_criteria.rationale: Excludes HSV encephalitis, structural lesions and overlapping demyelination before LP; it is normal in most patients and does not confirm the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lymphocytic pleocytosis (31 cells/uL), CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands and IgG index 0.78; HSV-1/2 PCR negative; CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (1:64) on cell-based assay
action_criteria.label: Analyze CSF for cells, protein and glucose, OCB/IgG index, HSV PCR and a cell-based IgG anti-GluN1 assay interpreted in parallel with serum
action_criteria.rationale: CSF anti-GluN1 IgG on a cell-based assay is the decisive test for definite disease, and HSV PCR addresses the can't-miss infectious mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Extreme delta brush, generalized rhythmic delta activity and three right temporal electrographic seizures with behavioural arrest
action_criteria.label: Obtain EEG for encephalopathic and epileptiform abnormalities, explicitly assessing for extreme delta brush
action_criteria.rationale: Staring spells, dyskinesias and fluctuating responsiveness need an EEG to separate seizures from movements; an abnormal EEG supports the diagnosis.

action_criteria.label: Screen for an ovarian teratoma with pelvic and abdominal ultrasound
action_criteria.rationale: Women of reproductive age carry the highest teratoma risk, and she had an ovarian cyst reported 2 years ago; tumour removal is part of first-line treatment.

action_criteria.label: Escalate to continuous EEG monitoring for seizure burden and non-convulsive seizures
action_criteria.rationale: Three electrographic seizures with behavioural arrest in a 40-minute EEG and fluctuating responsiveness: continuous EEG measures the seizure burden.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1-2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges).
Arrange prompt surgical removal of the left ovarian teratoma (laparoscopic, ovary-sparing where feasible) as part of first-line treatment, with gynaecology.
Treat seizures with an antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.

Admit to the ICU / neurocritical care for autonomic instability (heart rate to 128 bpm, blood pressure swinging from 105/62 to 158/96 mmHg with diaphoresis) and recurrent seizures, with airway assessment and cardiac monitoring.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioural management; gynaecology for the teratoma.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

differential.key_features: CSF HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR negative on an LP more than 72 hours after onset; MRI medial temporal and insular FLAIR signal without haemorrhage or restricted diffusion; CSF anti-GluN1 positive.

differential.diagnosis: Other antibody-mediated encephalitis (anti-LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B or AMPA receptor)
differential.key_features: Serum neuronal-surface panel negative (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, DPPX) and onconeural antibodies negative; mild hyponatraemia does not make LGI1 encephalitis likely with CSF anti-GluN1 positive.
Generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability, extreme delta brush and CSF pleocytosis with oligoclonal bands are not explained by a psychiatric disorder.

differential.diagnosis: Drug-induced psychosis or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
differential.key_features: No antipsychotic or illicit drug exposure; urine drug screen negative; CK only 262 U/L; rigidity and fever accompany seizures and dyskinesias.
ANA only weakly positive (1:40) with no rash, arthritis, cytopenia or other systemic feature; a maternal aunt with SLE does not change this; CSF anti-GluN1 explains the syndrome.

key_clinical_evidence: Subacute onset over about 10 days, after a viral-like prodrome, of anxiety and paranoia, pressured tangential speech with neologisms, generalized seizures, orofacial dyskinesias with chorea and rigidity, episodes of minimal responsiveness and autonomic instability: all six of the Graus 2016 groups.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titre 1:64) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:128 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows bilateral medial temporal (right greater than left) and right insular-opercular FLAIR signal without restricted diffusion, haemorrhage or enhancement; MRI is normal or non-specific in about two thirds and excludes structural causes, while the negative CSF HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.
EEG shows extreme delta brush with right temporal electrographic seizures; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows a 2.8 cm left ovarian mature cystic teratoma, probably the cyst reported 2 years ago: its removal is part of first-line treatment.
Earlier immunotherapy and tumour removal are associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia, an abnormal EEG and CSF pleocytosis accompany the psychiatric features and require exclusion of autoimmune encephalitis before a psychiatric diagnosis is accepted.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute psychiatric presentation (anxiety, insomnia, paranoid ideas about professors and classmates, bizarre night-time phone calls) in a student with no psychiatric history.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis (first-episode psychosis, brief psychotic disorder) and delays neurologic workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatraemia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing (SIADH from another cause, dehydration, polydipsia) instead of recognizing SIADH as a known complication of NMDAR-E.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: NMS needs antipsychotic exposure, which she has not had, and produces markedly raised CK with lead-pipe rigidity; a CK of 262 U/L here reflects the seizures and continuous dyskinesias and does not change management.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis when combined with dyskinesias and hyperthermia.

patient.history_present_illness: This 27-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman was brought to the emergency department by her roommate and campus police after ten days of escalating behavioral disturbance and two witnessed seizures. Approximately two and a half weeks before presentation, the patient experienced a self-limited febrile illness characterized by low-grade temperatures to 100.4 F, headache, myalgias, and fatigue lasting about five days, which she attributed to a 'stomach bug' and did not seek medical care. She appeared to recover fully, but a few days later her roommate began noticing subtle changes in her behavior: she became unusually anxious, had difficulty concentrating on coursework, and complained of persistent insomnia despite taking over-the-counter melatonin. Over the next several days, her condition deteriorated markedly. She became increasingly paranoid, convinced that her professors and classmates were conspiring against her, and she stopped attending classes. She began making bizarre, tangential phone calls to family members at all hours of the night. Her roommate observed her making repetitive chewing and lip-smacking movements, which the patient could not voluntarily suppress and did not seem aware of. Five days prior to presentation, her roommate witnessed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately two minutes, followed by prolonged confusion. Campus emergency services were called, and the patient was evaluated at a student health center, where she was given a dose of lorazepam 1 mg orally and referred to the emergency department, but the patient refused to go. Over the ensuing days, she became more disoriented, had a second generalized seizure witnessed by her roommate three days before presentation, and developed episodes of profuse sweating with fluctuating heart rates palpable by the roommate. On the morning of presentation, her roommate found her minimally responsive in bed with repetitive tongue movements and called 911. In the emergency department, the patient was agitated, intermittently combative, and exhibited florid orolingual dyskinesias and choreiform limb movements. She was unable to give any coherent history. Her roommate confirmed that there was no history of prior psychiatric illness, no recent travel, no new medications other than the melatonin, and no known substance use.

neurological_exam.additional: Prominent orolingual dyskinesias with stereotyped tongue protrusion and chewing movements present continuously. Intermittent choreiform and dystonic movements in bilateral upper extremities. Autonomic instability observed during the encounter: episodic tachycardia to 128 bpm, diaphoresis, and blood pressure fluctuations from 105/62 to 158/96 over a 20-minute period. Three brief episodes of staring with behavioral arrest and loss of responsiveness lasting 10-20 seconds observed during the encounter, raising concern for subclinical seizures.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing attempted but unreliable due to encephalopathy and superimposed involuntary movements; gross dysmetria not evident. Heel-to-shin not performed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Mild left lower facial weakness noted. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. Palate rises symmetrically. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculation. Prominent involuntary orolingual dyskinesias consisting of repetitive tongue protrusion, lip pursing, and chewing movements throughout the examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Not assessed; patient bed-bound due to encephalopathy and agitation requiring soft restraints.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but disoriented to time and situation. Intermittently agitated, alternating with episodes of staring and behavioral arrest lasting 10-20 seconds. Speech is pressured and tangential with frequent word-finding pauses and occasional neologisms. Unable to follow two-step commands reliably. Attempted Mini-Mental State Examination scored 14/30, with deficits in orientation, attention, recall, and language. Exhibits paranoid ideation, stating that hospital staff are 'poisoning' her. Short-term memory severely impaired.
neurological_exam.motor: Increased tone in all four extremities with cogwheel rigidity at the wrists bilaterally. Strength grossly 4+/5 in upper extremities, 5-/5 in lower extremities when the patient cooperates; assessment limited by encephalopathy and involuntary movements. No focal weakness pattern. Intermittent choreiform movements of the fingers and wrists bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor bilaterally. No ankle clonus.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws symmetrically to noxious stimuli in all extremities. Fine sensory testing unreliable due to altered mental status and poor cooperation.
